subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: The positioning here is unusually clear. “Chapel Hill Med Spa for Aesthetics & Longevity Medicine” names the town and stakes out a specific territory in one line, and the sentence beneath it — “medical-led aesthetic and wellness care in Chapel Hill designed to help you look, feel, and function at your best” — repeats the town and adds the medical framing. On desktop a solid black “Book Your Appointment” sits in the top right where it cannot be missed.

Two things work against it once the visitor is on a phone. That strong booking button moves into the menu, leaving only “Aesthetic Solutions” and “Wellness & Functional Medicine Solutions” visible — and both of those lead to more reading rather than an appointment. Below them the cookie panel takes the bottom third of the screen and covers the second one. The headline also runs to five lines at phone width, which pushes everything else down before the visitor has been given a reason to stay.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Positioning and local signals score close to full marks. Nearly everything lost is in proof and in what a phone visitor can actually reach.

scorecard.finding: Town and specialism named clearly in a single line.
“Medical-led” is stated, but no clinician, rating or review appears.
Excellent on desktop; on a phone the booking button is in the menu.
The two visible choices both lead to browsing rather than booking.
A five-line headline and a consent panel across the bottom third.
Chapel Hill named twice on the first screen.

strengthsLead: The positioning is the hardest thing on this list to get right, and it is already right.

strengths.title: The headline stakes out a specific territory.
strengths.body: “Chapel Hill Med Spa for Aesthetics & Longevity Medicine.” Longevity medicine is a real differentiator and naming it in the headline attracts a patient with a different, generally longer-term relationship than one booking a single treatment.

strengths.title: The town is named twice before the scroll.
strengths.body: Once in the headline and again in the supporting line. Proximity is the first filter an aesthetic patient applies, and it is answered here without them having to look for it.

strengths.title: “Medical-led” does real work.
strengths.body: It separates the practice from the beauty-salon end of the market in two words, and it sets up the longevity medicine claim rather than leaving it floating.

strengths.title: The desktop booking button is exactly where it should be.
strengths.body: Solid black, top right, permanently visible. Unmistakable, and it asks for the appointment rather than inviting a browse.

strengths.title: “At every stage of life” is well judged.
strengths.body: A quiet line that widens the audience without excluding anybody, and it sits naturally with the longevity positioning rather than being bolted on.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The headline names Chapel Hill and the specialism, with Book Your Appointment solid black in the top right.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. The headline runs to five lines, the booking button has moved into the menu, and the consent panel covers the lower third.

findings.heading: On a phone, neither visible button asks for the appointment.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the header carries the logo and a menu button; the desktop “Book Your Appointment” is not shown. The two buttons on the screen are “Aesthetic Solutions” and “Wellness & Functional Medicine Solutions”, and the second is partly covered by the consent panel.
findings.why: The one action that earns has been moved behind a menu button, and the two that remain lead to more reading. A patient who arrived ready to book must first find the menu, open it and look for the option — and every additional step loses a share of the people who were willing.
findings.recommended: Keep a compact Book Your Appointment in the mobile header beside the menu button. It is the single highest-value change on this list.

findings.heading: Nothing on the first screen can be checked by the visitor.
findings.evidence: No rating, review count, credential or named clinician appears on the opening screen, on either desktop or mobile. “Medical-led” does not say led by whom.
findings.why: The positioning is built on medical authority, and the page never shows the person that authority belongs to. Longevity medicine in particular is an area where patients are cautious about who is prescribing — and the practice is asking for that trust without introducing anybody.
findings.recommended: Name the physician with a photograph and qualification on the first screen, and add the Google rating with its review count beside the booking button. The medical positioning is the asset; a name is what makes it real.

findings.heading: The consent panel takes the bottom third of the phone screen.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the cookie notice begins immediately below the first button and continues past the foot of the screen, covering the lower half of the second button.
findings.why: It arrives at the moment the visitor is deciding, and it partially obscures one of only two available actions. A partly covered button also reads as a broken layout rather than a legal notice.
findings.recommended: Reduce it to a slim bar across the foot of the screen, keeping the same choices.

findings.heading: The headline runs to five lines at phone width.
findings.evidence: “Chapel Hill Med Spa for Aesthetics & Longevity Medicine” wraps across five lines in a large serif face, occupying roughly a third of the screen above the supporting sentence.
findings.why: The wording is good, but at that size it becomes a wall rather than a line, and it pushes the supporting sentence and both buttons further down. A headline that takes a third of the screen leaves little room for the reason to act.
findings.recommended: Reduce the mobile type size a step so it settles onto three lines. Same words, considerably more room beneath them.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Conventional and well built. The mobile menu behaves the way visitors expect.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: The buttons that are present are generous. The one that matters most is behind a menu on mobile.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No rating, review or credential appears anywhere near the point of decision.
“Medical-led” claims authority without showing anyone it belongs to.
On desktop, clear. On a phone the visitor is offered two ways to read more and no way to book.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Splitting aesthetics from wellness is a sensible way to sort visitors — it simply should not replace the booking action.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “At every stage of life” and “medical-led” are both measured and credible. There is very little overclaiming here, which is to the practice's credit.

roadmap.actions: Put Book Your Appointment in the mobile header. Reduce the consent panel to a slim bar. Drop the mobile headline a size so it settles onto three lines.
Name the physician with photograph and qualification on the first screen. Add the Google rating and review count beside the booking button.

Build authority content around the longevity medicine positioning — it is the differentiator and deserves depth. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 1366×768 and at 390 pixels wide, together with publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). The consent panel behaves differently for returning visitors who have already answered it.
